projects.title: Recover a repository you deliberately broke
projects.brief: Create a repo, wreck it four different ways, and get it back each time.
projects.why: Version control is only useful if you trust it under pressure. The way to trust it is to break things on purpose while nothing is at stake.
requirements: Create a repo with at least eight commits across two branches.
Cause a merge conflict and resolve it by hand, without a merge tool.
Hard reset away a commit, then recover it using the reflog.
Revert a commit that is already pushed, and explain why you did not reset.
Rewrite the last three commit messages with an interactive rebase.
Write a README section explaining, in your words, when each command is safe.
stretch: Add a pre-commit hook that refuses a commit with a syntax error.
Configure a .gitignore that survives adding a virtualenv by accident.
rubric: You can perform every recovery from memory, with no cheat sheet open.
You can say out loud what merge, revert, reset and rebase each do to history.
Nothing in the repo was lost that you did not intend to lose.

projects.title: A command-line expense tracker
projects.brief: A single-file CLI that records expenses, stores them, and reports totals.
projects.why: It exercises almost everything in the phase - input handling, data structures, files, errors - without needing any library at all.
requirements: Add, list and delete expenses from the command line.
Persist to a JSON file so data survives restarts.
Report totals by category and by month.
Reject bad input with a clear message rather than a traceback.
Handle a missing or corrupt data file without losing the good data.
No third-party dependencies. Standard library only.
stretch: Add a --since and --until date filter.
Export a month to CSV.
Add a simple text bar chart of spending per category.
rubric: It runs from a clean checkout by following the README alone.
Every behaviour you claim is covered by a test that fails when you break it.
The commit history shows the work, not one giant commit.
You can explain every design decision, including the ones you rejected.

projects.title: A text-adventure engine
projects.brief: A small game engine where rooms, items and exits are data, not code.
projects.why: The moment the map moves out of if-statements and into a dictionary, you have understood the difference between data and logic.
requirements: Rooms, exits and items are defined in a data file, not hard-coded.
The player can move, look, take, drop and check an inventory.
Unknown commands produce a helpful message, never a crash.
Game state can be saved and reloaded.
Adding a new room requires editing data only, not the engine.
stretch: Add locked doors that need a specific item.
Add a scripted ending condition.

projects.title: A log-processing pipeline that never loads the file
projects.brief: Process a multi-gigabyte log file with flat memory usage, and prove it.
projects.why: This is the exercise that makes generators click. You cannot fake it: either memory stays flat or it does not.
requirements: Generate a test log of at least 2 GB, or stream one you already have.
Parse, filter, and aggregate it through chained generators.
Peak memory stays roughly constant regardless of file size.
Prove it with a memory profile, and put the numbers in the README.
Provide a second, list-based implementation and compare the two.
Include a context manager that guarantees the file handle closes.
stretch: Add a --follow mode that tails a growing file.
Parallelise the aggregation and measure whether it actually helps.
rubric: It runs from a clean checkout by following the README alone.

projects.title: A small library with real protocols
projects.brief: A reusable package that implements the iterator, context manager and descriptor protocols rather than merely using them.
projects.why: Implementing a protocol is the fastest way to stop treating Python as magic and start reading the data model as an interface.
requirements: At least one custom iterator implemented without a generator.
At least one context manager, both as a class and via contextlib.
A decorator that preserves the wrapped signature and metadata.
Full type hints that pass a type checker with no ignores.
Docstrings on every public name, with a doctest that runs in CI.
stretch: Add a descriptor that validates attribute assignment.
Publish it to TestPyPI and install it in a fresh environment.

projects.title: A system health reporter
projects.brief: A command-line tool that reports disk, memory, process and service state, and exits non-zero when something is wrong.
projects.why: Automation that cannot be trusted by a monitoring system is a toy. An exit code is the difference.
requirements: Reports disk usage, load, memory and the top processes.
Thresholds are configurable, not hard-coded.
Exits 0 when healthy and non-zero when a threshold is breached.
Runs unattended from cron or a systemd timer.
Logs to a file with rotation, and never grows without bound.
Degrades gracefully when a metric is unavailable on this platform.
stretch: Add a --json mode for machine consumption.
Send an alert to a webhook, with retries and a rate limit.

A migration history, so the schema can be rebuilt from scratch.

projects.title: An automation engine that survives failure
projects.brief: A task runner that scrapes, transforms and stores data, and can be killed at any moment without losing or duplicating work.
projects.why: Anyone can write a script that works. The engineering is in what happens when the network, the site or the machine misbehaves.

Handles 429 and 5xx distinctly from 4xx.
Resumes after being killed mid-run, with no duplicated work.
Respects robots.txt and a configurable request rate.
Writes results to a database or structured files, atomically.
A dry-run mode that shows what it would do.
